docs.title: bipgen
docs.text:
bipgen is a convenient tool to generate spatial bipartite proximity graphs: two populations of nodes, called BCN (beacons) and TGT (targets), placed in the unit disk (2D) or the unit ball (3D), linked by edges whose probability decays with distance.

Graphs of this kind are the raw output of sequencing-based spatial methods, where molecular barcodes that end up close to each other get linked, and the spatial layout has to be inferred from the links alone. bipgen produces graphs in which every node has a known position, with sizes, degree distributions and spatial density that can be taken from an observed graph or simply specified by the user.

docs.title: The model in four steps
docs.text:
1. Positions: node positions are drawn uniformly or from a spatially correlated density, or given by the user.
  2. Target degrees: node degrees are drawn from a distribution or taken from an observed graph.
  3. Geometric edges: nodes are linked according to their distance. In the kernel model the probability of a link decays with distance and is adjusted so that the expected degrees match the targets. In the k-nearest-neighbour model each BCN is linked to its k nearest TGT, and degree targets are not used.
  4. Background edges: links unrelated to distance, which carry no information on how close two nodes are, added in a chosen proportion.

Everything is set by one YAML specification; a seed selects one realization of the ensemble it describes.

import bipgen

spec = bipgen.spec_from_dict({
    "sizes": {"n_bcn": 2000, "n_tgt": 3000},
    "degrees": {"distribution": "lognormal", "bcn": {"median": 15, "sigma": 0.5},
                "tgt": {"sigma": 0.6}},  # shape only: scale set by the BCN total
    "edges": {"model": "kernel", "kernel": "gaussian", "scale": 0.12},
    "background": {"model": "uniform", "ratio": 0.05},
})
graph = bipgen.generate(spec)          # seed 42 unless set otherwise
print(graph)
bipgen.plot_graph(graph)

Next: installation, the quickstart, and the model with its assumptions and known limitations.

docs.title: bipgen.graph.BipartiteGraph dataclass
docs.text:
A bipartite graph between side A (BCN, rows) and side B (TGT, columns).

geometric and background are disjoint (n_bcn, n_tgt) sparse matrices of 0/1 entries; their sum is the full biadjacency matrix. The data array of these matrices is the slot for edge weights in later versions. info records how the realization was produced: the seed, the target and expected numbers of edges, solver diagnostics, and the seconds spent in each step (timing). target_degrees holds the (bcn, tgt) target degrees of the kernel model, and is None for the kNN model.

docs.title: bipgen.plot.plot_comparison(table, ax=None)
docs.text:
z-score of each observed statistic within the ensemble; the band marks |z| <= 2.

Statistics with no spread in the ensemble have no z-score: they are drawn as hollow markers at 0 and labelled "no spread".

• Specification: one YAML file (or dictionary) per ensemble, with defaults and strict validation; default seed 42, overridable when generating; the seed used is recorded in every graph.
  • Positions: uniform in the unit disk or ball; spatially correlated densities in 2D and 3D, with cell counts arranged by Metropolis annealing to match a target correlogram (spatial correlation between nearby cells, Moran's I, at several lags); or given by the user.
  • Degrees: lognormal, constant or empirical target sequences, integer, with equal totals on the two sides.
  • Geometric edges: Gaussian kernel with node weights fitted by Sinkhorn scaling to the target degrees, sampled block by block; or each BCN linked to its k nearest TGT.
  • Background edges: uniform or proportional to the geometric degrees (the same share of background edges for every node on average), in a given ratio to the geometric edges; each edge records its origin.
  • Reproducibility: independent random streams spawned from one seed; Sinkhorn scaling on one BLAS thread, so results do not depend on the number of cores; every graph records the seconds spent in each generation step.
  • Observed graphs: specification from a biadjacency matrix (sizes, degree sequences, density of known positions); summary statistics and Monte Carlo comparison of an observed graph with an ensemble; Kolmogorov-Smirnov distances of degree distributions.
  • Input and output: native directory format, CSV edge lists.
  • Descriptors: registry with node degree and edge degree sum.
  • Presets: c58_4, c58_5, c58_16 from published Slide-recon arrays, and slidetags_tonsil from the Slide-tags human tonsil network.
  • Figures: layout in 2D and 3D, degree distributions, edge lengths, comparison with an ensemble.
  • Documentation: user guide, model with its literature sources, two tutorials.

Known limitations are listed in the documentation (The model and Observed graphs): clipping of probabilities at 1 lowers the degrees of dense nodes for short kernels; very short kernels prevent Sinkhorn scaling from converging; the kernel matrix is dense while it is fitted; the Poisson correction of a correlogram measured on points tends to overestimate it when the known points are a large fraction of the nodes.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
bipgen needs Python 3.10 or later. Its dependencies are NumPy, SciPy, pandas, Matplotlib, PyYAML and threadpoolctl.

pip install "git+https://github.com/FedericoScarpati/bipgen@v0.1.0"

This installs version 0.1.0 from GitHub and needs git. Without git, download the wheel attached to the release and install it with pip install bipgen-0.1.0-py3-none-any.whl. Version 0.1.0 was tested with Python 3.13, NumPy 2.5, SciPy 1.18, pandas 3.1 and Matplotlib 3.11, and with Python 3.10 and the newest versions of the dependencies available for it.

From a clone of the repository, in editable mode with the development tools:

git clone https://github.com/FedericoScarpati/bipgen
cd bipgen
pip install -e ".[dev]"
pytest

docs.title: Hardware requirements
docs.text:
• CPU: one realization runs on one core, in about half a minute for 27 000 x 19 000 nodes. Independent realizations can run in parallel processes.
  • Memory: fitting the kernel model holds one dense n_bcn x n_tgt matrix of 32-bit floats, about 2 GB for 27 000 x 19 000 nodes. Sampling works on row blocks.
  • Disk: a saved graph takes about 22 bytes per edge.

docs.title: Native format
docs.text:
bipgen.save(graph, path) writes one directory per graph:

File Content edges.csv bcn, tgt, origin (geometric or background) nodes.csv side, index, x, y (and z in 3D), target_degree (empty for the kNN model) spec.yaml, spec.npz the specification, and its arrays if any info.json seed and generation diagnostics

bipgen.load(path) reads it back.

docs.title: Edge lists
docs.text: bipgen.read_edge_list(path, bcn=..., tgt=...) reads a CSV file with integer node indices into a binary biadjacency matrix; repeated pairs are merged.

docs.title: The model
docs.text:
This page describes how bipgen builds one graph, in four steps: node positions, target degrees, geometric edges and background edges. For each step, the table gives the specification section that sets it and the attributes of the generated graph that hold its result; the text names each key where it acts. The last sections cover reproducibility and known limitations.

Step Set by Result Positions dim, sizes, positions graph.pos_bcn, graph.pos_tgt Target degrees degrees graph.target_degrees Geometric edges edges graph.geometric Background edges background graph.background Reproducibility seed graph.seed

The graph also keeps the specification it was built from, in graph.spec, and the diagnostics of each step, such as the correlogram reached or the Sinkhorn iterations, in graph.info, together with the seconds each step took (graph.info["timing"]).

docs.title: Positions
docs.text:
sizes.n_bcn BCN and sizes.n_tgt TGT are placed in the domain set by dim: the unit disk (dim: 2) or the unit ball (dim: 3). Lengths are in units of the domain radius. positions.method chooses one of three methods.

  • Uniform (uniform, the default). Points are spread uniformly over the domain.

  • Spatially correlated density (metropolis). Nodes are spread over a grid of cells, with a chosen variability of the counts between cells and a chosen correlation between nearby cells. BCN and TGT are drawn together from this density, then split at random.

    1. Grid: density.n_bins cells per axis, keeping the cells whose centre lies in the domain; 20 by default in 2D, 12 in 3D, where there are many more cells.
    2. Counts: one count per cell, drawn from density.occupancy, rescaled so that the counts add up to the number of nodes. With {source: gamma, cv: ...} the counts follow a Gamma distribution with coefficient of variation cv; with {source: file, key: ...} they are resampled from the array key of the arrays file, for instance measured on another graph (see Observed graphs).
    3. Arrangement: simulated annealing swaps the counts of two cells at a time, to bring the correlogram \(\rho_k\) towards the target \(\rho_k^\ast\) given by density.correlogram.
      • \(\rho_k\) is the spatial correlation between nearby cells (Moran's I [1]), computed over the pairs of cells \(k\) cells apart (distance between centres, rounded): lag 1 is the 8 surrounding cells in 2D, the 18 sharing a face or an edge in 3D.
      • A swap that changes the error \(E = \sum_k (\rho_k - \rho_k^\ast)^2\) by \(\Delta E\) is accepted with probability \(\min(1, e^{-\Delta E / T})\) (Metropolis rule). The temperature \(T\) starts where a worsening swap of average size is accepted with probability 0.8, and decreases geometrically to a thousandth of that over density.sweeps sweeps, of one proposed swap per cell.
      • Swaps keep the set of counts and change only their arrangement. The correlogram reached is stored in graph.info["correlogram"].
    4. Points: drawn uniformly inside each cell; points outside the domain are discarded, then random points are removed down to the exact total. The density is constant within each cell.

  • Given positions (file). Positions are read from two arrays of the arrays file, named by positions.bcn and positions.tgt, of shape (n_bcn, dim) and (n_tgt, dim); from Python, arrays can also be a dictionary of arrays. Positions are used as given, in the same units as edges.scale.

docs.title: Target degrees
docs.text:
Target degrees are used only by the kernel model, and are stored in graph.target_degrees. degrees.distribution sets the distribution, and degrees.bcn and degrees.tgt its parameters on each side:

  • lognormal: median median and standard deviation of the logarithm sigma; the TGT side takes only sigma;
  • constant: every BCN gets value;
  • empirical: positive values taken from the array key of the arrays file, resampled with replacement when their number differs from the number of nodes.

The BCN degrees are rounded and clipped to \([1, n_\mathrm{tgt}]\). The TGT values give only a shape: they are rescaled to the BCN total, rounded, clipped to \([1, n_\mathrm{bcn}]\) and adjusted by one unit at a time until the two totals are equal. With uniform and metropolis positions the order of the nodes carries no spatial information, so degrees are independent of position. With file positions, an empirical array as long as the side keeps its order: the \(i\)-th value goes to the \(i\)-th node.

docs.title: Geometric edges
docs.text:
Geometric edges depend on the distance \(d_{ij}\) between a BCN \(i\) and a TGT \(j\), and are stored in graph.geometric. Two models are available, set by edges.model:

  • kernel: each pair is linked at random, with probability \(P_{ij} = \min(1, \theta_i K(d_{ij}) \theta_j)\): the kernel \(K\) decays with distance, and the weights \(\theta\) of the nodes are fitted so that the expected degrees match the targets;
  • knn: each BCN is linked to its k nearest TGT, by distance alone.

docs.title: Kernel model
docs.text:
Each pair \((i, j)\) is linked independently with probability

\[ P_{ij} = \min\left(1,\ \theta_i \, K(d_{ij}) \, \theta_j\right), \]

where \(K\) is the kernel (see The kernel) and the node weights \(\theta\) solve

\[ \sum_j \theta_i K(d_{ij}) \theta_j = k_i, \qquad \sum_i \theta_i K(d_{ij}) \theta_j = k_j , \]

for every BCN \(i\) and every TGT \(j\), so that expected degrees match the targets \(k\) (before the clipping at 1, see Known limitations). The weights are found by Sinkhorn scaling [2], alternating \(\theta_i \leftarrow k_i / \sum_j K_{ij}\theta_j\) and \(\theta_j \leftarrow k_j / \sum_i K_{ij}\theta_i\), with \(K_{ij} = K(d_{ij})\), until no weight changes by more than edges.sinkhorn.tol, for at most edges.sinkhorn.max_iter iterations. graph.info records the iterations (sinkhorn_iterations), whether they converged (sinkhorn_converged) and the largest relative gap between expected and target degrees before clipping (sinkhorn_max_error).

docs.title: The kernel
docs.text:
The kernel \(K(d)\) is the profile of a link in distance. Each node has a weight \(\theta\), fitted to its target degree, and the kernel sets how far its links reach. A constant factor in \(K\) is absorbed by the weights, so only its shape matters, and \(K(0) = 1\). edges.kernel names the kernel. The only kernel in this version is the Gaussian:

  • Gaussian (gaussian):

    \[ K(d) = e^{-(d/L)^2}, \]

    where \(L\) is edges.scale, in units of the domain radius. The kernel depends on the distance only through \(d/L\): it falls to \(1/e \approx 0.37\) at \(d = L\) and to \(e^{-4} \approx 0.02\) at \(d = 2L\), so \(L\) is the reach of a link. The Gaussian is the profile of a molecule that diffuses for a fixed time from one node towards the other, and \(L\) is the distance it typically travels in that time: as is standard for diffusion processes, \(L^2 = 4Dt\) for a diffusion coefficient \(D\) and a time \(t\).

docs.title: k-nearest-neighbour model
docs.text: Each BCN is linked to its edges.k nearest TGT. BCN degrees are exactly k; TGT degrees follow from the geometry, and the degrees section is not used.

docs.title: Background edges
docs.text:
Background edges link pairs regardless of distance, and are stored in graph.background. Their number is background.ratio times the number of geometric edges, rounded down; graph.info["background_ratio"] records the ratio reached. background.model sets how the endpoints are drawn:

  • none (the default): no background edges;
  • uniform: every pair equally likely;

  • configuration: pair \((i, j)\) drawn with probability proportional to the geometric degrees of its nodes,

    \[ \Pr(i, j) \propto g_i\, g_j, \qquad g_i = \text{number of geometric edges of } i, \]

    so that every node gets on average the same share of background edges, ratio / (1 + ratio). Nodes without geometric edges get none.

Pairs that are already linked are redrawn, so the two kinds of edges are disjoint; the origin column of graph.edges() tells them apart.

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text: One seed spawns independent random streams for positions, degrees, geometric edges and background edges (numpy.random.SeedSequence). The seed is seed in the specification (default 42), generate(spec, seed=...) overrides it, and graph.seed records the one used. Sinkhorn scaling runs on one BLAS thread, so its result does not depend on the number of cores. On a given machine and library build the same seed gives the same graph.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
• Clipping lowers degrees. Sinkhorn scaling matches the targets before the clipping at 1. For kernels short compared with the distance between linked nodes, clipping removes edges: with 800 x 1000 nodes, lognormal degrees with BCN median 15 and sigma 0.5 (BCN) and 0.6 (TGT), and uniform positions, the expected number of edges is 90% of the target at scale 0.15 and 99% at scale 0.30. Broader degree distributions lose more. graph.info reports target_edges, the target number of edges, and expected_edges, the expected number after clipping.
  • Short kernels. When too few partners lie within the kernel range, the weights keep growing and Sinkhorn scaling stops at edges.sinkhorn.max_iter with a warning, also kept in graph.info["warning"]; if they overflow, generation stops with an error. Increase edges.scale or lower the degrees.
  • Memory. The kernel matrix is dense during scaling (\(4\,n_\mathrm{bcn} n_\mathrm{tgt}\) bytes).
  • Densities are measured on 2D points only: spec_from_graph accepts planar positions, while generation works in 2D and 3D. Measurement in 3D is planned for a future version.
  • Densities measured on points carry the assumptions listed in Observed graphs.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. P. A. P. Moran, Notes on continuous stochastic phenomena, Biometrika 37, 17 (1950).
  2. R. Sinkhorn, A relationship between arbitrary positive matrices and doubly stochastic matrices, Ann. Math. Statist. 35, 876 (1964).

docs.title: From a graph to a specification
docs.text:
spec_from_graph builds a kernel-model specification from a biadjacency matrix (BCN as rows, TGT as columns):

import bipgen

adj = bipgen.read_edge_list("edges.csv", bcn="bcn", tgt="tgt")
spec = bipgen.spec_from_graph(adj, scale=0.15)
spec.save("observed.yaml")      # writes observed.yaml and observed.npz

What is read off the graph:

  • the number of nodes and the degree sequence of each side, after binarizing the matrix and dropping isolated nodes; they become an empirical degree section;
  • if positions of some nodes are given, the cell occupancies and the correlogram of their density (see below); positions are then drawn with the Metropolis method.

What is not inferred, and has to be chosen: the kernel scale and the background.

docs.title: Density measured on points
docs.text:
With positions, spec_from_graph takes the 2D points, maps their bounding box to \([-1, 1]^2\), counts the points in the cells of a grid with n_bins cells per axis inside the disk, and computes the spatial correlation between nearby cells (Moran's I) of the counts at lags 1 to n_lags. This assumes that the known positions are a random sample of the nodes, and that BCN and TGT share the same density, since both are drawn from it.

Correction for partial positions

When the known points are only part of the nodes, counting noise attenuates the correlation. spec_from_graph uses the corrected correlogram, multiplied by \(\mathrm{var}/(\mathrm{var} - \mathrm{mean})\) (Poisson counts around the density), or the raw one when the correction is not usable. The correction tends to overestimate the correlation when the known points are a large fraction of the nodes, and is unstable when cells hold few points.

docs.title: Comparing an observed graph with an ensemble
docs.text:
ensemble = [bipgen.generate(spec, seed=s) for s in range(20)]
table = bipgen.compare(adj, ensemble)
bipgen.plot_comparison(table)
bipgen.degree_ks(adj, ensemble)

statistics computes, on the observed graph and on each realization alike: numbers of nodes and edges, mean, median, 90th percentile and maximum degree of each side, and the fraction of nodes in the largest connected component. Only nodes with at least one edge are counted. compare reports the observed value, the ensemble mean and standard deviation, the z-score and the percentile of the observed value in the ensemble: a Monte Carlo goodness-of-fit check. degree_ks compares the degree distributions with the two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance, next to the distance between two realizations, which is what sampling alone produces.

compare also accepts a stored summary instead of a graph, such as bipgen.presets.observed(name).

docs.title: Presets
docs.text:
import bipgen

bipgen.presets.available()                 # ['c58_16', 'c58_4', 'c58_5', 'slidetags_tonsil']
spec = bipgen.presets.load("c58_4")
graph = bipgen.generate(spec)              # about half a minute on one core
table = bipgen.compare(bipgen.presets.observed("c58_4"), [graph])

docs.title: Presets
docs.text:
Specifications built from published datasets with bipgen.spec_from_graph.

Preset Source dataset c58_4, c58_5, c58_16 Slide-recon arrays c58_4, c58_5, c58_16 (Hu et al., Nature Biotechnology 2025; Single Cell Portal SCP2577) slidetags_tonsil Slide-tags human tonsil (Russell et al., Nature 2024; Single Cell Portal SCP2169), cell-bead network as used in Dahlberg et al., Nature Communications 16, 9652 (2025)

The code of bipgen is distributed under the package license. The preset data are derived from the datasets above and follow the terms of their sources: the Single Cell Portal terms of service for the Slide-recon arrays and the Slide-tags data (research use), and CC BY 4.0 for the cell-bead network of Dahlberg et al. Please cite the source papers when using a preset.

What is taken from the data:

  • sizes and degree sequences of the observed graph, with counts binarized and isolated nodes dropped (degrees_bcn, degrees_tgt in the .npz);
  • cell occupancies and correlogram (lags 1 and 2) of the known BCN positions on a 20 x 20 grid, with the Poisson correction for counting noise (see Observed graphs in the documentation); these drive the Metropolis positions. Only part of the BCN have a known position and no TGT does: the presets assume that known positions are a random sample of the nodes and that BCN and TGT share the same density.

What is chosen by hand, not inferred from the data:

  • the Gaussian kernel and its scale, 0.15 domain radii;
  • no background edges.

<name>_observed.json holds the summary statistics of the observed graph, so that bipgen.compare(bipgen.presets.observed(name), ensemble) works without the raw data.

With scale 0.15, clipping probabilities at 1 lowers the expected number of edges below the observed one (seed 42, one realization each):

Preset Expected edges / observed edges c58_4 0.995 c58_5 0.892 c58_16 0.964 slidetags_tonsil 0.998

c58_16 and slidetags_tonsil deserve care. In c58_16 BCN and TGT appear to be distributed differently in space; in slidetags_tonsil the two sides are cell nuclei and beads, which are distributed differently too. The presets draw both sides from one shared density.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text: Step What it does Functions 1. Describe Describe the ensemble, in a specification load_spec, spec_from_dict, presets.load, spec_from_graph 2. Generate Generate one realization per seed generate 3. Inspect Inspect contents, figures graph.edges(), plot_graph, plot_degrees 4. Compare Compare with an observed graph compare, degree_ks 5. Save Save to disk and read back save, load

docs.title: 1. Describe
docs.text:
Describe the specification of a desired graph in a YAML file, or a dictionary of YAMLs with the same layout. Unknown keys are rejected, so a typo raises an error instead of being ignored.

import bipgen

spec = bipgen.load_spec("my_spec.yaml")
# or
spec = bipgen.spec_from_dict({
    "sizes": {"n_bcn": 2000, "n_tgt": 3000},
    "degrees": {"distribution": "lognormal", "bcn": {"median": 15, "sigma": 0.5},
                "tgt": {"sigma": 0.6}},  # shape only: scale set by the BCN total
    "edges": {"model": "kernel", "kernel": "gaussian", "scale": 0.12},
})
  • From a preset, built from published data: bipgen.presets.load("c58_4"). See Presets.
  • From an observed graph: sizes and degrees are read off its biadjacency matrix. See Observed graphs.
adjacency = bipgen.read_edge_list("edges.csv")
spec = bipgen.spec_from_graph(adjacency, scale=0.15)

See Specification format for every field.

docs.title: 2. Generate
docs.text:
graph = bipgen.generate(spec)            # seed from the specification, default 42
other = bipgen.generate(spec, seed=7)    # another realization of the same ensemble
ensemble = [bipgen.generate(spec, seed=s) for s in range(10)]

The seed actually used is stored in graph.seed and graph.info["seed"]. The same seed gives the same graph.

docs.title: 3. Inspect
docs.text:
Contents

graph.pos_bcn, graph.pos_tgt       # positions, (n, dim) arrays
graph.geometric, graph.background  # disjoint (n_bcn, n_tgt) sparse 0/1 matrices
graph.biadjacency                  # all edges
graph.edges()                      # table: bcn, tgt, origin
graph.degrees()                    # realized degrees of both sides
graph.target_degrees               # targets of the kernel model
graph.info                         # seed, edges, solver diagnostics, seconds per step

Figures

bipgen.plot_graph(graph)          # nodes and a subset of edges, 2D or 3D
bipgen.plot_degrees(graph)        # realized and target degree distributions
bipgen.plot_edge_lengths(graph)   # edge lengths by origin

docs.title: 4. Compare
docs.text:
table = bipgen.compare(adjacency, ensemble)   # observed value, ensemble mean, sd, z-score
bipgen.plot_comparison(table)
bipgen.degree_ks(adjacency, ensemble)         # degree distributions

Statistics are computed in the same way on the observed graph and on each realization. See Observed graphs.

docs.title: 5. Save
docs.text:
bipgen.save(graph, "out/graph_042")      # edge table, node table, specification
again = bipgen.load("out/graph_042")

See Saving and loading. The tutorials go through all of this with figures.

docs.title: Specification format
docs.text:
A specification is a YAML file (or a dictionary with the same layout) that fully determines an ensemble of graphs. Arrays, such as empirical degree sequences or given positions, live in an optional .npz file next to it, referenced by arrays; from Python, arrays can also be a dictionary of arrays.

All lengths are in units of the domain radius: the domain is the unit disk in 2D and the unit ball in 3D. Unknown keys raise SpecError.

docs.title: Top level
docs.text: Key Default Meaning seed 42 default seed; generate(spec, seed=...) overrides it dim 2 dimension of the domain: 2 (unit disk) or 3 (unit ball) sizes required n_bcn, n_tgt: number of nodes of each side positions uniform see below degrees required for the kernel model, absent for knn see below edges required see below background none see below arrays null companion .npz file, relative to the YAML file, or a dictionary of arrays schema 0 version of the format (compatibility check)

docs.title: positions
docs.text:
The density keys are used only with method: metropolis; see The model.

Key Values Meaning method uniform, metropolis, file uniform in the domain, a spatially correlated density, or given positions density.n_bins default 20 in 2D, 12 in 3D cells per axis of the grid on which the density is built density.occupancy {source: gamma, cv: 0.5} or {source: file, key: ...} how many nodes each cell holds: drawn from a Gamma distribution with coefficient of variation cv (larger cv, more uneven cells), or taken from counts in the arrays file density.correlogram default [0.3, 0.1] how alike nearby cells are: target spatial correlation between nearby cells (Moran's I), for cells 1, 2, ... cells apart; 0 means no spatial structure, values towards 1 give large smooth patches density.sweeps default 400 length of the annealing that arranges the cells; one sweep proposes one swap per cell bcn, tgt array names with file: the (n_bcn, dim) and (n_tgt, dim) position arrays, in the same units as edges.scale

docs.title: degrees
docs.text:
Target degrees are integers, and the totals of the two sides are equal. The TGT distribution only gives a shape: its scale follows from \(n_\mathrm{bcn} \langle k_\mathrm{bcn} \rangle = n_\mathrm{tgt} \langle k_\mathrm{tgt} \rangle\).

distribution bcn tgt lognormal median, sigma sigma constant value (empty) empirical key (array in the .npz) key

Empirical sequences are resampled with replacement when their length differs from the number of nodes. Degrees are assigned to nodes at random.

docs.title: edges
docs.text: Key Meaning model kernel (degree-matched kernel model) or knn kernel name of the kernel; only gaussian in this version scale kernel length \(L\) (see The kernel), required with kernel sinkhorn optional solver settings: tol, the iterations stop when no node weight changes by more than this (default 1e-3); max_iter (default 2000) k with knn: each BCN links to its k nearest TGT; there is no degrees section

docs.title: background
docs.text: Key Meaning model none, uniform (endpoints uniform), configuration (endpoints proportional to their geometric degrees: every node gets the same share of background edges on average) ratio background edges per geometric edge

docs.title: Example file
docs.text:
# Example bipgen specification (schema 0).
# One file fully determines an ensemble; a seed picks one realization.
# Units: the domain is the unit disk (dim 2) or the unit ball (dim 3);
# every length below is in units of the domain radius.

schema: 0          # version of this format
seed: 42           # default 42; generate(spec, seed=...) overrides it, and the
                   # seed actually used is always recorded in the output graph
dim: 2             # 2 or 3

sizes:
  n_bcn: 5000      # nodes of side A (rows of the biadjacency matrix)
  n_tgt: 5000      # nodes of side B (columns)

positions:
  method: uniform  # uniform | metropolis | file
  # metropolis only: node counts on a grid with n_bins cells per axis, clipped to
  # the disk or ball, rearranged by simulated annealing to bring their spatial
  # correlation towards the target correlogram.
  # density:
  #   n_bins: 20                            # 12 by default in 3D
  #   occupancy: {source: gamma, cv: 0.5}   # or {source: file, key: occupancy}
  #   correlogram: [0.30, 0.10]            # correlation between cells 1, 2 cells apart
  #   sweeps: 400                           # one swap proposed per cell per sweep
  # file only: names of the (n_bcn, dim) and (n_tgt, dim) arrays in the arrays file
  # bcn: pos_bcn
  # tgt: pos_tgt

degrees:           # target degrees (integers), matched in expectation by Sinkhorn scaling
  distribution: lognormal   # lognormal | constant | empirical
  bcn: {median: 20, sigma: 0.5}
  tgt: {sigma: 0.5}         # shape only: both sides must have the same total,
                            # so n_bcn * <k_bcn> = n_tgt * <k_tgt> fixes the TGT scale
  # constant:  bcn: {value: 20}, tgt: {}
  # empirical: bcn: {key: degrees_bcn}, tgt: {key: degrees_tgt}  (resampled, TGT rescaled)
  # Degrees are assigned to positions at random (no degree-position correlation).

edges:
  model: kernel    # kernel | knn
  kernel: gaussian # name in the kernel registry
  scale: 0.10      # kernel length L: K(d) = exp(-(d / L)^2)
  # sinkhorn: {tol: 1.0e-3, max_iter: 2000}   # optional solver settings
  # knn only: each BCN links to its k nearest TGT (degrees section ignored)
  # k: 10

background:        # edges unrelated to distance, drawn after the geometric ones
  model: uniform   # none | uniform | configuration (endpoints ~ geometric degrees)
  ratio: 0.05      # background edges per geometric edge

arrays: null       # optional companion .npz with the arrays referenced above

docs.title: Building a specification in Python
docs.text:
Only what differs from the defaults has to be given; spec.to_dict() shows the full specification, with the defaults filled in.

import bipgen

spec = bipgen.spec_from_dict({
    "sizes": {"n_bcn": 2000, "n_tgt": 3000},
    "degrees": {"distribution": "lognormal", "bcn": {"median": 15, "sigma": 0.5},
                "tgt": {"sigma": 0.6}},  # shape only: scale set by the BCN total
    "edges": {"model": "kernel", "scale": 0.12},
})
spec.save("my_spec.yaml")
spec = bipgen.load_spec("my_spec.yaml")

Arrays can be passed directly as a dictionary, here for given positions; save then writes them to an .npz file next to the YAML file.

spec = bipgen.spec_from_dict({
    "sizes": {"n_bcn": 2000, "n_tgt": 3000},
    "positions": {"method": "file", "bcn": "pos_bcn", "tgt": "pos_tgt"},
    "edges": {"model": "knn", "k": 5},
    "arrays": {"pos_bcn": pos_bcn, "pos_tgt": pos_tgt},   # (2000, 2) and (3000, 2)
})
spec.save("given.yaml")                                    # given.yaml + given.npz

docs.title: Getting started¶
docs.text: This tutorial builds a specification, draws graphs from it with different seeds and specifications, compares them, and saves one. It runs in a few seconds.

docs.title: A specification¶
docs.text: A dictionary with the layout of the YAML format: 2000 BCN and 3000 TGT in the unit disk, lognormal target degrees, a Gaussian kernel of scale 0.12 and 5% background edges.

docs.title: One realization¶
docs.text: The seed comes from the specification (42 by default) unless it is given in the call. info records the seed, the target number of edges, the expected number after clipping probabilities at 1, the convergence of Sinkhorn scaling, and the seconds spent in each step (timing).

docs.title: Seeds¶
docs.text: The same seed gives the same graph; other seeds give other realizations of the same ensemble.

docs.title: Different specifications¶
docs.text: The same sizes and degrees with a short kernel, a long one, and the long one with more background edges. Sinkhorn scaling matches the target degrees before probabilities are clipped at 1: with the short kernel, clipping removes part of the edges, and expected_edges measures it.

docs.title: Comparing graphs¶
docs.text: One row per graph: nodes and a subset of edges, edge lengths, and the degree distributions of the two sides, realized against target. A longer kernel gives longer edges; background edges have lengths unrelated to distance and add to the degrees.

docs.title: k nearest neighbours¶
docs.text: Each BCN links to its k nearest TGT; no degree section is needed.

docs.title: Spatially correlated density¶
docs.text: Cell counts with coefficient of variation 0.8, arranged to bring the spatial correlation between nearby cells (Moran's I) at lags 1 and 2 towards the target. The correlogram reached is in info.

docs.title: 3D¶
docs.text: The domain becomes the unit ball.

docs.title: Saving¶
docs.text: One directory per graph: edge table, node table, specification and diagnostics.

The realizations have about 0.4% fewer edges than the observed graph: this is the loss from clipping probabilities at 1 (expected_edges above). Realizations differ from each other so little that this small gap is many standard deviations. Clipping also caps the largest degrees, which stay below the observed maxima. Statistics with no spread in the ensemble, such as the numbers of nodes, have no z-score.

Degree distributions: the distance from the observed degrees, next to the distance between two realizations, which is what sampling alone produces.

docs.title: Presets and comparison with observed graphs¶
docs.text: The presets are specifications built from published Slide-recon arrays. This tutorial draws a few realizations of one of them and compares them with the summary of the observed graph. Generating a full-size graph takes about half a minute on one core, so the whole notebook takes a couple of minutes.

docs.title: An ensemble¶
docs.text: Three realizations: enough to see the spread, not to estimate tails.

docs.title: Comparison with the observed graph¶
docs.text: presets.observed holds the statistics and degree sequences of the observed graph, so the comparison does not need the raw data. The z-score places the observed value in the ensemble.

docs.title: A specification from your own graph¶
docs.text: spec_from_graph takes a biadjacency matrix (BCN as rows, TGT as columns) and reads off sizes and degree sequences; the kernel scale and the background are chosen by hand. Here a generated graph stands in for an observed one. With known positions of some nodes (positions=), the density is measured as well and positions are drawn with the Metropolis method.
